title: Polynomial Regression Quiz
description: Test your understanding of polynomial regression

questions.question: How does polynomial regression model non-linear relationships?
options: By using a non-linear optimization algorithm
By transforming features into polynomial terms and applying linear regression
By creating multiple linear models and combining them
By using a curved loss function
questions.explanation: Polynomial regression creates polynomial features (x, x², x³, etc.) from the original features and then applies standard linear regression to these transformed features. This allows modeling non-linear relationships while using the linear regression framework.

questions.question: What happens when you use a polynomial degree that is too high for your data?
options: The model will underfit and have high training error
The model will overfit, fitting noise in the training data
The model will train faster
The model will become more interpretable
questions.explanation: Using a polynomial degree that is too high leads to overfitting. The model will fit the training data very closely, including noise, resulting in a wiggly curve that doesn't generalize well to new data. This is characterized by low training error but high test error.

questions.question: Why is feature normalization especially important for polynomial regression?
options: It makes the model train faster
Polynomial features have vastly different scales (x vs x¹⁰), causing numerical instability
It improves the R² score
It reduces the number of features needed
questions.explanation: Polynomial features can have vastly different scales. For example, if x=10, then x²=100 and x¹⁰=10 billion. These different scales cause numerical instability and slow convergence in gradient descent. Normalization ensures all features have similar scales.

questions.question: For a dataset with a quadratic (parabolic) relationship, what is the minimum polynomial degree needed to fit it well?
options: Degree 1 (linear)
Degree 2 (quadratic)
Degree 3 (cubic)
Degree 5 or higher
questions.explanation: A quadratic relationship requires at least degree 2 to capture the parabolic shape. Degree 1 would underfit (straight line can't capture a curve), while higher degrees would work but add unnecessary complexity.

questions.question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff in polynomial regression?
options: Higher degree increases bias and decreases variance
Higher degree decreases bias but increases variance
Degree doesn't affect bias or variance
Higher degree increases both bias and variance
questions.explanation: As polynomial degree increases, the model becomes more flexible (lower bias - can fit more complex patterns) but also more sensitive to training data variations (higher variance - overfitting). The goal is to find the degree that balances these two.

questions.question: If your polynomial regression model has very low training error but high test error, what is the likely problem?
options: The learning rate is too high
The model is underfitting
The model is overfitting - degree is too high
The features need to be normalized
questions.explanation: Low training error but high test error is the classic sign of overfitting. The model has learned the training data too well, including noise, and doesn't generalize to new data. Reducing the polynomial degree or adding regularization can help.

questions.question: What is a major limitation of polynomial regression for extrapolation (predicting beyond the training data range)?
options: It's too slow for large datasets
Polynomial curves can shoot off to extreme values outside the training range
It can't handle missing values
It requires too much memory
questions.explanation: Polynomial curves, especially high-degree ones, can behave erratically outside the training data range, often shooting off to very large positive or negative values. This makes polynomial regression unreliable for extrapolation beyond the observed data.

questions.question: How should you start when selecting a polynomial degree for a new problem?
options: Always use the highest degree possible
Start with degree 1 and never increase it
Start with a low degree (2-3) and increase if needed based on validation performance
Randomly select a degree between 1 and 10
questions.explanation: The best practice is to start simple with degree 2 or 3, then increase if the model underfits. Use cross-validation to evaluate different degrees and choose the one that balances training and validation performance. This prevents overfitting while ensuring adequate model complexity.
